items.title: Nasdaq Drops Friday But Ends the Week Up: Stock Market Today
items.summary:

Looking ahead, there's plenty on next week's docket to keep markets volatile, including Nvidia's ( NVDA ) first earnings report without Jensen Huang at the helm and the highly anticipated Anthropic IPO .

At the close, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was down 0.9% at 25,136 and the broader S&P 500 was off 0.4% at 7,561. The blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average finished up 0.1% at 52,347.

Ahead of the open, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the Producer Price Index (PPI), which measures wholesale prices, rose 0.3% from September to October — lower than economists' 0.4% forecast. But PPI was up 6.5% year over year, the highest annual rate since November 2022.

Core PPI, which excludes volatile food and energy costs, rose 0.3% month over month, in line with expectations. However, core PPI's annual rate of 5% was the highest since January 2023.

"The good news is that producer price inflation cooled from September," says Chris Osmond , chief investment officer for Fifth Third Wealth Advisors. "The bad news is that it may not have cooled enough to give markets the rate relief they want." 

Indeed, rate-hike odds rose after this morning's PPI. According to CME Group FedWatch , futures traders are now pricing in a 90% probability the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates by a quarter-percentage point at its December meeting, up from 85% one day ago.

items.title: Microsoft Outage Scams Are Coming: What to Watch for
items.summary:
Yesterday, a Microsoft outage that took down Outlook, Teams and other critical tools disrupted work and daily life for millions. The major tech company is still working out the issues and, as of this writing, Microsoft 365 products for both business and consumers are still experiencing service degradation . 

The widespread disruption has not only made work difficult, it's left millions vulnerable to a flurry of scams targeting Microsoft users . 

Eric Hulse, Vice President of Research and Development at Command Zero , an AI Security Operations Center, has seen similar scams happen in previous outages. When CrowdStrike went down in 2024, for example, Hulse says the company's own team members were sent malware under the guise of software that would "fix" the issue.

As you await word on progress or next steps from Microsoft, it's important to be wary of some of the most common types of online scams that tend to pop up during and after widespread outages.

What kind of scams should you watch for after the Microsoft outage? When it comes to scams built around widespread events like this, fraudsters take advantage of what people are trying to do next, according to Eric Hulse. "They want to fix the problem, get back into their account, reach support or get compensated, and there's a fake version of each."

The common scams you might see include:

Lookalike websites designed to steal your password and other information Fake support websites Calls or emails requesting access to accounts Promises of refunds for those affected by the outage Phishing links for restoring affected…

items.title: What Inflation and High Prices Mean for Your Retirement
items.summary:
In 1989, Honey, I Shrunk the Kids introduced moviegoers to Wayne Szalinski, an absent-minded inventor whose experimental shrinking machine accidentally reduced his children to a fraction of their normal size.

More than three decades later, many Americans may feel as though someone has aimed a similar machine at their checkbooks. The culprit, of course, is inflation .

If you've bought groceries , paid an insurance bill, eaten at a restaurant, filled your gas tank or written a tuition check recently, you don't need an economist to tell you that things cost considerably more than they did five or six years ago.

Consider what happened during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Massive fiscal and monetary stimulus, supply-chain disruptions, labor shortages and pent-up consumer demand combined to create the highest inflation America had experienced in four decades. 

For much of 2021, government and Federal Reserve officials characterized the surge in inflation as "transitory," expecting the rate of inflation to return toward normal relatively quickly. But by June 2022, the Consumer Price Index had risen 9.1% over the previous year.

While inflation has subsequently declined significantly, that doesn't mean prices have gone back to where they started.

items.title: 5 Everyday Health Habits That Save $100,000+ in Retirement
items.summary:
Eating healthy and exercising may help you live longer and also save you tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, of dollars in retirement healthcare costs.

That should be welcome news given that out-of-pocket expenses are poised to skyrocket, increasing nearly 50% by 2050. Medical debt is already a main cause of bankruptcy among Americans and a leading reason retirees say they have to dip into their savings more than expected. Healthcare expenses also make up a large share of retirees' costs, even after accounting for Medicare .

So what does staying healthy really mean? Medical experts point to several key habits, including:

Regular aerobic and strength training. The standard recommendation for adults 50 and older is 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week and two strength training workouts each week. 

Adopting an anti-inflammatory diet. Eating a diet rich in leafy greens, berries, lean proteins and whole grains supports cardiovascular health and lowers the risk of cognitive decline.

Prioritizing restorative sleep. Consistently getting 7 to 9 hours of quality sleep per night helps the body and mind heal. 

Maintaining social connections and cognitive stimulation. Regular social engagement and learning new skills lower the risk of dementia.

Maintaining healthy markers. Keeping blood pressure, blood glucose, and cholesterol levels within target ranges helps prevent chronic illnesses, strokes and mobility issues.

But how much can you really save by adopting a healthy lifestyle? Read on to find out.

items.title: Ask the Editor: Questions on IRAs and Year-End Tax Planning
items.summary:
Each week in our Ask the Tax Editor series, Joy Taylor, The Kiplinger Tax Letter editor, answers questions on topics submitted by readers. This week, she's looking at four tax questions from readers on year-end tax planning strategies involving IRAs and other retirement accounts. ( Get a free issue of The Kiplinger Tax Letter or subscribe .) 

1. Late-year withholding from an IRA Question: I am retired, and most of my income is from required minimum distributions (RMDs) from traditional IRAs and 401(k) plans, Social Security, and dividends and capital gains from taxable investments. I heard that I don't have to make quarterly estimated tax payments and that instead I can wait until year-end and ask my IRA custodian to withhold a lump sum amount of income tax from my year-end IRA distribution to satisfy my federal income tax liability for the year. Is that true?

Joy Taylor: Pretty much, yes. For federal income tax purposes, tax withheld at any point in the year is treated as if evenly paid throughout the year. Some retirees rely on this rule to have federal income taxes that they expect to owe for a year withheld from November and/or December RMDs from their traditional IRAs instead of making quarterly estimated tax payments.

For IRA distributions, federal law requires that the IRA custodian withhold 10% for federal income tax withholding unless you tell the custodian otherwise. 
For example, you can tell your custodian you don't want any withholding, or you can request that as much as 100% be withheld.

items.title: Why You Shouldn’t Let Political Dread Dictate Your Portfolio
items.summary:
The midterm election season has delivered a live demonstration of the market volatility that can emerge when investors trade elections. 

The day after Democrats won control of both the House and Senate, the Dow jumped 3% , its best post-midterm day since 1982. A day later, stocks plummeted , and semiconductors plunged more than 12%, their worst day since the COVID-19 crash. 

The volatility playing out in markets is not particularly abnormal, for election seasons are often erratic. In 2020, stocks posted their worst week since the March sell-off of that year the week before the election, then their best election week since 1932. 

In 2022's midterm season, stocks rose before the vote, plummeted after, then rallied hard to end the week. Stocks nerves going into the 2024 election also proved fleeting, with the market staging a historically strong surge second only to the 2020 rally in the week after the election.

Investors appear to be once again falling into what has become a common pattern of allowing politics to spook their portfolio strategy, despite the fact that in all of those recent cases, investor nerves around elections proved unsupported. 

A positive outlook Stocks were up at least 15% in the year after each of the last three elections. Probabilities favor a positive outlook in general — stocks have risen in the year after elections nearly 75% of the time since 1928. Likewise, U.S. stocks tend to rise regardless of which party holds the White House or how Congress is split.

Just look at the divergence in performance between the chipmaker and the broader market. NVDA stock is off more than 30% from the all-time high it notched in October. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 is down only about 2.5% from its own record high.

Instead, investors are freaking out about one company. They're not exactly abandoning all things AI.

"As for the broader AI trade, this is an NVIDIA problem before it is an AI problem," writes Mark Malek , chief investment officer at Siebert Financial. "The biggest buyers are funding this buildout out of their own cash flow, and they need the chips no matter whose name is on the door."

items.title: Car Insurance Review: 8 Things to Check to Save Money
items.summary:
When your car insurance premium comes due, do you simply pay it without giving your coverage much thought? If so, you're not alone. Most drivers just pay their premiums unless it's time to file a claim or their rates increase. That could be an expensive mistake, since a simple car insurance review might help you save money on your policy . 

A lot can change in a year. You might drive less, have paid off your vehicle or qualify for discounts that you weren't eligible for previously. You might be overpaying for insurance, and if you simply renew your policy, you could continue overpaying for months or years. 

Before your next payment, take time for a car insurance review and consider these questions to make sure your current policy still works for you. 

1. Are you paying for coverage you no longer need? Though nearly all states require drivers to carry liability coverage, collision and comprehensive coverage are optional. Collision insurance helps repair or replace your vehicle if it's damaged in an accident, and comprehensive coverage helps repair or replace your vehicle if a non-collision event, like weather or vandalism, damages it.

If your vehicle is older and has depreciated, it may no longer make sense to buy collision and comprehensive coverage. On the other hand, these coverages may be worth the extra expense if you have a newer or more expensive vehicle that would be costly to replace. 

If you have a car loan or lease, review the terms before changing your insurance. Lenders and leasing companies may require you to maintain a certain amount of collision and…
items.t: Car Insurance Review: 8 Things to Check to Save Money

Why AI purchases can be your responsibility

"It's the new refund trap," Aaron Painter, CEO of Nametag and author of Deepfaked , told Kiplinger. "If you authorize AI to act, the banks view it as your responsibility."

items.title: Is Your Diversified Portfolio Just an Illusion?
items.summary:
Wise investing calls for diversifying your portfolio , so that's what people try to do.

They spread their money among several stocks. They add bonds because bonds are supposed to be the "safe" part. They toss in mutual funds and exchange-traded funds. For a little principal protection, they may include a CD and a savings account. And then they relax because they think diversification has been achieved.

But it's often an illusion.

Take a closer look at those investments and you'll see they have something in common. Other than the CD and savings account, they're all bought and sold in the same markets, priced by the same market forces and exposed to the same fundamental risk. Bonds may feel safer than stocks, but they are still market investments, with no guarantee of principal.

2022 proved the point. The S&P 500 lost roughly 18% that year, and the broad U.S. bond market fell about 13%, one of its worst years on record. Investors who counted on bonds to cushion a stock decline watched both fall together.

True diversification, in its most meaningful sense, requires assets that are not highly correlated. In other words, assets whose values do not rise and fall together in response to the same conditions.

Fortunately, there is a way to pursue true diversification: Spread your investments among three worlds — the Market World, the Protection World and the Alternative World. At our firm, we refer to this trio of options as the Triversified™ Approach.

items.title: What to Expect When You Inherit an HSA
items.summary:
There's a reason health savings accounts (HSAs) are often hailed as one of the best financial tools out there. Many people are used to enjoying the tax savings that come with traditional and Roth retirement plan contributions. HSAs combine those benefits into a single account that’s loaded with flexibility.

HSA contributions are tax-deductible (or made pre-tax through payroll), and you can invest unused funds tax-free. Withdrawals used for qualified medical expenses are tax-free, too. And at age 65, penalties for non-medical HSA withdrawals disappear. At that point, an HSA can double as a traditional IRA or 401(k), where withdrawals are taxable but can be taken for any purpose. 

While an HSA can be beneficial during your lifetime, it's not always an ideal account to pass along to heirs.

Spouses can still reap the benefits Inheriting an HSA remains advantageous if it's your spouse’s account. 

"The good news is that for a spouse who inherits an HSA, it keeps being an HSA," says Evan Mills, financial adviser at Scholar Advising . "They can use it for their qualified medical expenses, exactly the way it's designed."

Susan Einberger, CFP and owner of Enjoy the Ride: Financial + Life Planning , says taking over an HSA as a spouse is simple.

"The surviving spouse completes tax form 8889 as though the HSA belonged to them," she explains.

Non-spouse beneficiaries can face tax headaches Just as inheriting an IRA can come with rules, the same is true with an HSA. But an HSA may come with more tax consequences. 

"A non-spouse heir doesn't really inherit an HSA," says Mills.…
items.t: What to Expect When You Inherit an HSA

items.title: How to Protect an Aging Parent’s Finances Without Conflict
items.summary:
Every winter, the mail brings a 1099-DIV. It reports dividends and takes about four seconds to understand.

Another "DIV," the one that can shape a family's next decade, never arrives in an envelope. It shows up in a phone call that begins, "Something happened to dad."

That DIV is dignity, identity and vulnerability — an acronym I've developed over decades advising families through some of their most sensitive planning moments. It is a simple framework I regularly use to help families move these conversations from crisis management to thoughtful preparation.

In fact, I have rarely seen an estate plan fail because the documents were poorly drafted. I have often seen one fail because no one had the hard conversation while mom or dad was still fully in charge.

Documents don't fail families. Timing does.

You can use the same framework to help aging family members preserve their sense of autonomy. I'd urge you to address each part before a crisis forces the conversation.

items.title: High-Asset Divorce: A Financial Survival Guide
items.summary:
If you're a fan of Bravo or have watched The Real Housewives of New York , you likely know Sonja Morgan's story. 

Once married to financier John Adams Morgan, a great-grandson of J.P. Morgan, she went through a high-profile divorce and has spent years navigating life on her own terms as a business owner and public figure.

It is easy to focus on the headlines, but Sonja's situation reflects a much more common reality. Divorce , especially after a high-asset marriage, does not simplify a financial life. It often makes it significantly more complex. 

There may be substantial assets on paper, but those assets can come with liquidity challenges, ongoing obligations and the need to build a new financial identity.

That transition is not just about dividing assets . It is about understanding them, managing them and making independent decisions about what comes next.

As an attorney and financial planning strategist at Carson Group , when I work with clients going through a divorce like this, one of the first things we clarify is what they actually have. That sounds simple enough, but it is often far more complex than it sounds.

items.title: The $1,100 Myth About Car Insurance You Need to Stop Believing
items.summary:
You get your car insurance renewal offer and see higher rates than last year despite making no claims and no other changes to your policy. In frustration, you think about switching, but it doesn't seem easy and who knows if you'll even get a better quote elsewhere. 

It is a common misconception that switching car insurance is hard. In this year's Kiplinger Readers' Choice Awards survey, dozens of respondents complained of rising premiums and declining customer service but said the idea of shopping around seemed "overwhelming," "painful" or "high pressure." 

"I'd like to look elsewhere but it's not easy to do," said one Kiplinger reader. In today's digital age, however, shopping around for better rates is easier than ever. And continuing to believe this myth about the difficulty of switching car insurance can cost you hundreds of dollars each year – not a price worth paying at a time when all of your other bills are going up, too. 

The "switching car insurance is complicated" myth is costing you hundreds Whenever I get a renewal letter, it takes me only one hour to get multiple quotes and either switch or leverage those offers to get a better rate from my existing insurance provider. 

My car insurance policy is up for renewal every six months, so I shop it twice a year. This year alone, I've switched both times, saving a little over $500 each time. That's a total savings of just over $1,100 over the year for about two hours of work. 

My experience isn't unusual. According to Insurify , customers who shop around save up to $1,100 annually on average. In fact, many state…
items.t: The $1,100 Myth About Car Insurance You Need to Stop Believing

items.title: How to Secure Your Right to a VA National Cemetery Resting Place
items.summary:
Honoring military service means ensuring veterans — and their families — receive every benefit they have rightfully earned. Among the most significant yet frequently overlooked of these honors is the right to a final resting place in a VA national cemetery.

Each year, only 15% of all eligible veterans who die are interred in a VA national cemetery , while about 5% opt for a State, Territorial or Tribal Veterans cemetery, according to the National Cemetery Administration (NCA). In 2025, the NCA conducted 130,963 interments and provided approximately 495,951 Presidential Memorial Certificates to families.

Prequalifying for a veteran's funeral through the Department of Veterans Affairs' " pre-need eligibility determination " program allows families to clear administrative paperwork long before it is needed.

Who gets the VA funeral benefit? 

(Image credit: Getty Images) Burial benefits in a VA national cemetery are available to veterans, service members, and certain family members. NCA data show that the number of veterans interred at VA cemeteries rose from 36,422 in 1973 to 130,963 in 2025. 

Roughly 15.7 million people, or almost 6% of the population, are military veterans, according to the Census Bureau . Almost 31% of veterans are 75 or older. 

Who can be buried in a veterans cemetery : 

Veterans and service members: Any member of the Armed Forces who meets active-duty service requirements and whose last discharge or separation was under conditions other than dishonorable. Members of the National Guard and Reserve also qualify if they meet the guidelines . Spouses…
items.t: How to Secure Your Right to a VA National Cemetery Resting Place

items.title: Should the 2026 Midterm Sweep Change Your Estate Plan?
items.summary:
Whenever control of Congress shifts in Washington, wealthy families and financial advisers inevitably ask the same high-stakes question: Is it time to rewrite our financial playbook? 

With Democrats winning control in the midterm elections , it's not a bad idea for high-net-worth households to rethink some of their tax strategies. But does that mean you need to completely change your estate plan? Not necessarily.

There's no need to panic It's natural to be concerned about the midterm election results, says T.L. Turnipseed, head of personal trusts at Alta Trust Company . But he doesn't think there's a reason to be alarmed.

As a quick refresher, current law puts the estate tax exemption at $15 million per person, or up to $30 million for a married couple. The exemption, Turnipseed says, is indexed for inflation and carries no built-in expiration date.

However, Turnipseed warns, Congress can change these "permanent" tax codes. 

"The election itself changes nothing," he says, "but a Congress controlled by the other party could lead to exemptions being revisited." 

"Families with estates well above the exemption should treat a reduction as a scenario to prepare for." — T.L. Turnipseed

Kelsey Simasko, attorney at Simasko Law , isn't particularly worried about near-term estate tax changes. 

"A study by the Pew Research Center shows that the 2025 to 2026 congressional session was one of the least productive sessions in terms of laws passed in the last 40 years," she says. "As a citizen, I would hope this new Congress can rally and become more productive, but I do not think…
items.t: Should the 2026 Midterm Sweep Change Your Estate Plan?

items.title: AI Apps and Tools for Older Adults at Home
items.summary:
The wide world of so-called age tech — devices, apps and services designed to help older adults navigate life — can seem dazzling at first. 

Wearing a pendant with a button to summon emergency help is no longer cutting edge. Now there are 4D radar imaging home sensors that alert caregivers when you fall (or lie immobile for too long); "smart mats" you can stand on to check your vital signs; a tabletop AI robot that can play games or remind you to take your meds — and more.

Whether you're considering a few innovations for your own comfort, or you want to make life easier and safer for a loved one, these systems promise peace of mind, and even light entertainment, for all involved. But where do you begin?

First, keep an open mind when it comes to "age tech" — a trendy term — versus other kinds of technology that might also be useful to you, says Laurie Orlov, who tracks industry research and trends in the Aging, Health and Technology Watch blog. "Start by identifying the problem you want to solve, because that will help you find more products specific to your particular need," she advises.

Why technology matters more with age People are living longer (no surprise there). But 93% of adults age 65 and up live in their own home or apartment, according to the Pew Research Center , and 60% hope to keep it that way by continuing to age in place with the help of a caregiver. 

This is both a noble aim and a tall order, given that two-thirds of people will need long-term care at some point in their lives. And given the strain on people's time and energy, it's no surprise that…
items.t: AI Apps and Tools for Older Adults at Home

items.title: Budget-Friendly Holiday Tips
items.summary:
The holidays are right around the corner, and inflation has pinched budgets with rising gas prices, electricity costs, and more.

As such, it isn't surprising that people plan to spend and travel less this holiday season. NerdWallet recently released its 2026 Holiday Spending report , which found that those surveyed plan to spend 21% less on gifts this holiday season. 

While there's a lot of pressure to spend during the holidays, there are smart strategies you can use to enjoy the season, spend less, and avoid looking like a Grinch.

1. Set a holiday spending cap early 

(Image credit: Getty Images) Before making a list of the gifts you want to buy, establish a budget . This helps you determine how much you can spend without relying on a credit card, since the last thing you want is a hefty credit card bill in January.

On this front, here are some tips to help you:

Make a list: Create a list of everyone you want to buy gifts for and how much you plan to spend on each. As part of this list, include other holiday-related expenses, such as travel, concerts, family gatherings and meals. Check it twice: As you buy gifts or incur other holiday expenses, review your budget to ensure you're within your spending limit. If expenses are higher than anticipated, adjust your budget to reduce spending on remaining gifts and expenses. One way I make the holidays more affordable is by buying gifts throughout the year. It makes the holidays much less stressful since I spread my expenses out. While this might not be practical advice now, it could help you down the road.

items.title: From blood group ID to cycle racks: I asked for little ways to fix broken Britain and the public’s ideas give me hope | Martin Lewis
items.summary:
There are thousands of small tips to make our country better. People know what is wrong, and it’s clear they have solutions

Have you ever come across an annoying little problem and thought, “why don’t they just fix that?” If so, I want to hear from you. I’m looking for your ideas for practical, low-cost, non-controversial ways to improve the UK – whether that’s health, schools, transport, business, housing, policing, justice, tech, shopping, money – or owt else entirely.

The spark for this happened just over a year ago, when I spoke at Politico’s fringe event at Labour’s conference. The key discussion was about Keir Starmer’s unpopularity. I was asked what I’d have advised the government when it took power, so I said: “Come up with 100 small things that piss people off and that you can fix, and they can see that you have fixed them.” Then I reeled off a list of small fixes for my subject area: the counterproductive way council tax debt is escalated; renaming “tax-free childcare”; and so on.

Tell people their blood group at their first adult blood test. Knowing you’ve a common or rare type may make you more inclined to donate. It’s a brilliantly simple nudge that could widen the donor pool and save lives.

A mandatory “AI-edited” label on property photos on estate agency sites.

items.title: The Guardian view on rough sleeping: Burnham’s laudable target is in danger of being missed | Editorial
items.summary:
Energetic mayors and councils can help street homeless people to rebuild their lives. But the underlying affordability crisis needs tackling too

Bringing an end to rough sleeping was among Andy Burnham’s first pledges after entering Downing Street – as it was when he became mayor of Manchester. With temperatures dropping, and frosts expected, winter night shelters across the UK are up and running. But an ongoing acute shortage of suitable housing and the latest tranche of early prisoner releases mean ministers know that the prime minister’s laudable target is in danger of being missed.

The official figures are shocking. There were 8,748 rough sleepers in England in June, an increase of about 1,000 since January (Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland collect data separately). These are among the most vulnerable people in society, both in terms of past experiences and future prospects, including drastically curtailed life expectancy. The complex and sometimes chaotic situations of people who end up on the streets, most of whom are men, mean that helping them is challenging. Family breakdown, substance misuse, mental…
